pieces.text: . Henry David Thoreau opens his book by explaining his motivations for writing about his solitary life near Walden Pond and his subsequent return to society. He also shares some observations about people in Concord.

textContent.text: When I wrote the following pages, or rather the bulk of them, I lived alone, in the woods, a mile from any neighbor, in a house which I had built myself, on the shore of Walden Pond, in Concord, Massachusetts, and earned my living by the labor of my hands only. I lived there two years and two months. At present I am a sojourner in civilized life again.

I should not obtrude my affairs so much on the notice of my readers if very particular inquiries had not been made by my townsmen concerning my mode of life, which some would call impertinent, though they do not appear to me at all impertinent, but, considering the circumstances, very natural and pertinent. Some have asked what I got to eat; if I did not feel lonesome; if I was not afraid; and the like. Others have been curious to learn what portion of my income I devoted to charitable purposes; and some, who have large families, how many poor children I maintained. I will therefore ask those of my readers who feel no particular interest in me to pardon me if I undertake to answer some of these questions in this book.

pieces.text: , or first person, is omitted; in this it will be retained; that, in respect to egotism, is the main difference. We commonly do not remember that it is, after all, always the first person that is speaking. I should not talk so much about myself if there were anybody else whom I knew as well. Unfortunately, I am confined to this theme by the narrowness of my experience. Moreover, I, on my side, require of every writer, first or last, a simple and sincere account of his own life, and not merely what he has heard of other men's lives; some such account as he would send to his kindred from a distant land; for if he has lived sincerely, it must have been in a distant land to me. Perhaps these pages are more particularly addressed to poor students. As for the rest of my readers, they will accept such portions as apply to them. I trust that none will stretch the seams in putting on the coat, for it may do good service to him whom it fits.

textContent.text: I would fain say something […], something about your condition, especially your outward condition or circumstances in this world, in this town, what it is, whether it is necessary that it be as bad as it is, whether it cannot be improved as well as not. I have traveled a good deal in Concord; and everywhere, in shops, and offices, and fields, the inhabitants have appeared to me to be doing penance in a thousand remarkable ways. […] The twelve labors of Hercules¹ were trifling in comparison with those which my neighbors have undertaken; for they were only twelve, and had an end; but I could never see that these men slew or captured any monster or finished any labor. […]

I see young men, my townsmen, whose misfortune it is to have inherited farms, houses, barns, cattle, and farming tools; for these are more easily acquired than got rid of. But men labor under a mistake. The better part of the man is soon ploughed into the soil for compost. By a seeming fate, commonly called necessity, they are employed, as it says in an old book, laying up treasures which moth and rust will corrupt and thieves break through and steal. It is a fool's life, as they will find when they get to the end of it, if not before.
<sub>1. In Greek mythology, the twelve labors are difficult tasks that Hercules has to complete as a punishment.</sub>
Adapted from Henry David Thoreau, Walden

content.text: In 1845, twenty-seven-year-old Henry David Thoreau embarked on a unique experiment by moving to Walden Pond in Massachusetts.

pieces.text: Thoreau built a small cabin on land owned by his friend and mentor Ralph Waldo Emerson and lived there for over two years.

content.text: His goal was not just to live in solitude but to explore a simpler, more deliberate way of life, closely attuned to nature.

textContent.text: Thoreau wrote extensively during his time at Walden Pond, keeping a journal full of observations about nature and his reflections about life. He also wrote lectures that he delivered to audiences in Concord as a response to people's curious questions about his solitary lifestyle.

content.text: These writings formed the basis of the book
a collection of eighteen essays eventually published in 1854. These essays explore the themes of work, leisure, self-sufficiency, and the natural world.

pieces.text: , Thoreau contributed significantly to American literature and philosophy by challenging contemporary social norms and offering profound insights on what it means to be human.

contents.text: In the passage, Thoreau explains his choice to write using first-person narration and the personal pronoun "I."  However, he argues that no matter whether an author uses first-person or third-person narration, it is always the author, or "the first person," who is speaking either way. This illustrates Thoreau's opinion that books always reflect their writers' points of view, even if they do not use first-person narration.

contents.text: Here, Thoreau likens his book to a coat that will fit some and not others. The line "it may do good service to him whom it fits" suggests that Thoreau's writings will be useful and meaningful to those who can naturally relate to them. The line, "I trust that none will stretch the seams in putting on the coat," cautions against stretching the meaning of the book too far.
So, the bolded text shows Thoreau's hope that readers of his book will embrace the parts relevant to them without stretching the meaning of the rest to suit their own expectations.

contents.text: A sojourner is a temporary resident, or someone who is just passing through. By describing himself as a sojourner in civilized life, Thoreau indicates that he views himself as a visitor in polite society, and that he views nature as his permanent residence. And by using the term "at present," he suggests that the future might be different, leaving open the possibility that he might leave society again someday. This self-description suggests that he views his time in society as just a brief visit, not a permanent residence, and leaves open the possibility that he might someday leave it again.

I see young men, my townsmen, whose misfortune it is to have inherited farms, houses, barns, cattle, and farming tools; for these are more easily acquired than got rid of.

contents.text: In the passage, Thoreau points out that his neighbors are always busy with work that society expects them to do. He compares their tasks to the "twelve labors of Hercules" but argues that unlike Hercules's work, the neighbors' work does not end with any significant achievement. This constant work stops them from doing things that might make them happier or more fulfilled. Thoreau notes at the end that the burden of this work is then passed on to the next generation.
So, Thoreau implies that societal obligations may become burdens that prevent people from pursuing more fulfilling paths.

textContent.text: When I wrote the following pages, or rather the bulk of them, I lived alone, in the woods, a mile from any neighbor, in a house which I had built myself, on the shore of Walden Pond, in Concord, Massachusetts, and earned my living by the labor of my hands only. I lived there two years and two months. At present I am a sojourner in civilized life again.

I should not obtrude my affairs so much on the notice of my readers if very particular inquiries had not been made by my townsmen concerning my mode of life, which some would call impertinent, though they do not appear to me at all impertinent, but, considering the circumstances, very natural and pertinent. Some have asked what I got to eat; if I did not feel lonesome; if I was not afraid; and the like. Others have been curious to learn what portion of my income I devoted to charitable purposes; and some, who have large families, how many poor children I maintained. I will therefore ask those of my readers who feel no particular interest in me to pardon me if I undertake to answer some of these questions in this book.

We commonly do not remember that it is, after all, always the first person that is speaking. I should not talk so much about myself if there were anybody else whom I knew as well. Unfortunately, I am confined to this theme by the narrowness of my experience. Moreover, I, on my side, require of every writer, first or last, a simple and sincere account of his own life, and not merely what he has heard of other men's lives; some such account as he would send to his kindred from a distant land; for if he has lived sincerely, it must have been in a distant land to me. Perhaps these pages are more particularly addressed to poor students. As for the rest of my readers, they will accept such portions as apply to them. I trust that none will stretch the seams in putting on the coat, for it may do good service to him whom it fits.

textContent.text: I would fain say something […], something about your condition, especially your outward condition or circumstances in this world, in this town, what it is, whether it is necessary that it be as bad as it is, whether it cannot be improved as well as not. I have traveled a good deal in Concord; and everywhere, in shops, and offices, and fields, the inhabitants have appeared to me to be doing penance in a thousand remarkable ways. […] The twelve labors of Hercules¹ were trifling in comparison with those which my neighbors have undertaken; for they were only twelve, and had an end; but I could never see that these men slew or captured any monster or finished any labor. […]

I see young men, my townsmen, whose misfortune it is to have inherited farms, houses, barns, cattle, and farming tools; for these are more easily acquired than got rid of. But men labor under a mistake. The better part of the man is soon ploughed into the soil for compost. By a seeming fate, commonly called necessity, they are employed, as it says in an old book, laying up treasures which moth and rust will corrupt and thieves break through and steal. It is a fool's life, as they will find when they get to the end of it, if not before.
<sub>1. In Greek mythology, the twelve labors are difficult tasks that Hercules has to complete as a punishment.</sub>
Adapted from Henry David Thoreau, Walden

alternativeText.text: A black and white photograph of Henry David Thoreau

content.text: In 1845, twenty-seven-year-old Henry David Thoreau embarked on a unique experiment by moving to Walden Pond in Massachusetts.

pieces.text: Thoreau built a small cabin on land owned by his friend and mentor Ralph Waldo Emerson and lived there for over two years.

content.text: His goal was not just to live in solitude but to explore a simpler, more deliberate way of life, closely attuned to nature.

textContent.text: Thoreau wrote extensively during his time at Walden Pond, keeping a journal full of observations about nature and his reflections about life. He also wrote lectures that he delivered to audiences in Concord as a response to people's curious questions about his solitary lifestyle.

content.text: These writings formed the basis of the book
a collection of eighteen essays eventually published in 1854. These essays explore the themes of work, leisure, self-sufficiency, and the natural world.

pieces.text: , Thoreau contributed significantly to American literature and philosophy by challenging contemporary social norms and offering profound insights on what it means to be human.

contents.text: In the passage, Thoreau explains his choice to write using first-person narration and the personal pronoun "I."  However, he argues that no matter whether an author uses first-person or third-person narration, it is always the author, or "the first person," who is speaking either way. This illustrates Thoreau's opinion that books always reflect their writers' points of view, even if they do not use first-person narration.

[…] The twelve labors of Hercules¹ were trifling in comparison with those which my neighbors have undertaken; for they were only twelve, and had an end; but I could never see that these men slew or captured any monster or finished any labor. […]

I see young men, my townsmen, whose misfortune it is to have inherited farms, houses, barns, cattle, and farming tools; for these are more easily acquired than got rid of. But men labor under a mistake. The better part of the man is soon ploughed into the soil for compost. By a seeming fate, commonly called necessity, they are employed, as it says in an old book, laying up treasures which moth and rust will corrupt and thieves break through and steal. It is a fool's life, as they will find when they get to the end of it, if not before.
<sub>1. In Greek mythology, the twelve labors are difficult tasks that Hercules has to complete as a punishment.</sub>
Adapted from Henry David Thoreau, Walden

textContent.text: When I wrote the following pages, or rather the bulk of them, I lived alone, in the woods, a mile from any neighbor, in a house which I had built myself, on the shore of Walden Pond, in Concord, Massachusetts, and earned my living by the labor of my hands only. I lived there two years and two months. At present I am a sojourner in civilized life again.

I should not obtrude my affairs so much on the notice of my readers if very particular inquiries had not been made by my townsmen concerning my mode of life, which some would call impertinent, though they do not appear to me at all impertinent, but, considering the circumstances, very natural and pertinent. Some have asked what I got to eat; if I did not feel lonesome; if I was not afraid; and the like. Others have been curious to learn what portion of my income I devoted to charitable purposes; and some, who have large families, how many poor children I maintained. I will therefore ask those of my readers who feel no particular interest in me to pardon me if I undertake to answer some of these questions in this book.

contents.text: Here, Thoreau likens his book to a coat that will fit some and not others. The line "it may do good service to him whom it fits" suggests that Thoreau's writings will be useful and meaningful to those who can naturally relate to them. The line, "I trust that none will stretch the seams in putting on the coat," cautions against stretching the meaning of the book too far.
So, the bolded text shows Thoreau's hope that readers of his book will embrace the parts relevant to them without stretching the meaning of the rest to suit their own expectations.

content.text: At present I am a sojourner in civilized life again.

contents.text: A sojourner is a temporary resident, or someone who is just passing through. By describing himself as a sojourner in civilized life, Thoreau indicates that he views himself as a visitor in polite society, and that he views nature as his permanent residence. And by using the term "at present," he suggests that the future might be different, leaving open the possibility that he might leave society again someday. This self-description suggests that he views his time in society as just a brief visit, not a permanent residence, and leaves open the possibility that he might someday leave it again.

contents.text: In the passage, Thoreau points out that his neighbors are always busy with work that society expects them to do. He compares their tasks to the "twelve labors of Hercules" but argues that unlike Hercules's work, the neighbors' work does not end with any significant achievement. This constant work stops them from doing things that might make them happier or more fulfilled. Thoreau notes at the end that the burden of this work is then passed on to the next generation.
So, Thoreau implies that societal obligations may become burdens that prevent people from pursuing more fulfilling paths.

content.text: In 1845, twenty-seven-year-old Henry David Thoreau embarked on a unique experiment by moving to Walden Pond in Massachusetts.

pieces.text: Thoreau built a small cabin on land owned by his friend and mentor Ralph Waldo Emerson and lived there for over two years.

content.text: His goal was not just to live in solitude but to explore a simpler, more deliberate way of life, closely attuned to nature.

textContent.text: Thoreau wrote extensively during his time at Walden Pond, keeping a journal full of observations about nature and his reflections about life. He also wrote lectures that he delivered to audiences in Concord as a response to people's curious questions about his solitary lifestyle.

content.text: These writings formed the basis of the book
a collection of eighteen essays eventually published in 1854. These essays explore the themes of work, leisure, self-sufficiency, and the natural world.

pieces.text: , Thoreau contributed significantly to American literature and philosophy by challenging contemporary social norms and offering profound insights on what it means to be human.

contents.text: In the passage, Thoreau explains his choice to write using first-person narration and the personal pronoun "I." textContent.text: I would fain say something […], something about your condition, especially your outward condition or circumstances in this world, in this town, what it is, whether it is necessary that it be as bad as it is, whether it cannot be improved as well as not. I have traveled a good deal in Concord; and everywhere, in shops, and offices, and fields, the inhabitants have appeared to me to be doing penance in a thousand remarkable ways. […] The twelve labors of Hercules¹ were trifling in comparison with those which my neighbors have undertaken; for they were only twelve, and had an end; but I could never see that these men slew or captured any monster or finished any labor. […]

I see young men, my townsmen, whose misfortune it is to have inherited farms, houses, barns, cattle, and farming tools; for these are more easily acquired than got rid of. But men labor under a mistake. The better part of the man is soon ploughed into the soil for compost. It is a fool's life, as they will find when they get to the end of it, if not before.

content.text: At present I am a sojourner in civilized life again.

contents.text: A sojourner is a temporary resident, or someone who is just passing through. By describing himself as a sojourner in civilized life, Thoreau indicates that he views himself as a visitor in polite society, and that he views nature as his permanent residence. And by using the term "at present," he suggests that the future might be different, leaving open the possibility that he might leave society again someday. This self-description suggests that he views his time in society as just a brief visit, not a permanent residence, and leaves open the possibility that he might someday leave it again.

contents.text: In the passage, Thoreau points out that his neighbors are always busy with work that society expects them to do. He compares their tasks to the "twelve labors of Hercules" but argues that unlike Hercules's work, the neighbors' work does not end with any significant achievement. This constant work stops them from doing things that might make them happier or more fulfilled. Thoreau notes at the end that the burden of this work is then passed on to the next generation.
So, Thoreau implies that societal obligations may become burdens that prevent people from pursuing more fulfilling paths.

[…] The twelve labors of Hercules¹ were trifling in comparison with those which my neighbors have undertaken; for they were only twelve, and had an end; but I could never see that these men slew or captured any monster or finished any labor. […]

I see young men, my townsmen, whose misfortune it is to have inherited farms, houses, barns, cattle, and farming tools; for these are more easily acquired than got rid of. But men labor under a mistake. The better part of the man is soon ploughed into the soil for compost. By a seeming fate, commonly called necessity, they are employed, as it says in an old book, laying up treasures which moth and rust will corrupt and thieves break through and steal. It is a fool's life, as they will find when they get to the end of it, if not before.
<sub>1. In Greek mythology, the twelve labors are difficult tasks that Hercules has to complete as a punishment.</sub>
Adapted from Henry David Thoreau, Walden

content.text: In 1845, twenty-seven-year-old Henry David Thoreau embarked on a unique experiment by moving to Walden Pond in Massachusetts.

pieces.text: Thoreau built a small cabin on land owned by his friend and mentor Ralph Waldo Emerson and lived there for over two years.

content.text: His goal was not just to live in solitude but to explore a simpler, more deliberate way of life, closely attuned to nature.

textContent.text: Thoreau wrote extensively during his time at Walden Pond, keeping a journal full of observations about nature and his reflections about life. He also wrote lectures that he delivered to audiences in Concord as a response to people's curious questions about his solitary lifestyle.

content.text: These writings formed the basis of the book
a collection of eighteen essays eventually published in 1854. These essays explore the themes of work, leisure, self-sufficiency, and the natural world.

pieces.text: , Thoreau contributed significantly to American literature and philosophy by challenging contemporary social norms and offering profound insights on what it means to be human.

pieces.text: . Henry David Thoreau opens his book by explaining his motivations for writing about his solitary life near Walden Pond and his subsequent return to society. He also shares some observations about people in Concord.

textContent.text: When I wrote the following pages, or rather the bulk of them, I lived alone, in the woods, a mile from any neighbor, in a house which I had built myself, on the shore of Walden Pond, in Concord, Massachusetts, and earned my living by the labor of my hands only. I lived there two years and two months. At present I am a sojourner in civilized life again.

I should not obtrude my affairs so much on the notice of my readers if very particular inquiries had not been made by my townsmen concerning my mode of life, which some would call impertinent, though they do not appear to me at all impertinent, but, considering the circumstances, very natural and pertinent. Some have asked what I got to eat; if I did not feel lonesome; if I was not afraid; and the like. Others have been curious to learn what portion of my income I devoted to charitable purposes; and some, who have large families, how many poor children I maintained. I will therefore ask those of my readers who feel no particular interest in me to pardon me if I undertake to answer some of these questions in this book.

pieces.text: , or first person, is omitted; in this it will be retained; that, in respect to egotism, is the main difference. We commonly do not remember that it is, after all, always the first person that is speaking. I should not talk so much about myself if there were anybody else whom I knew as well. Unfortunately, I am confined to this theme by the narrowness of my experience. Moreover, I, on my side, require of every writer, first or last, a simple and sincere account of his own life, and not merely what he has heard of other men's lives; some such account as he would send to his kindred from a distant land; for if he has lived sincerely, it must have been in a distant land to me. Perhaps these pages are more particularly addressed to poor students. As for the rest of my readers, they will accept such portions as apply to them. I trust that none will stretch the seams in putting on the coat, for it may do good service to him whom it fits.

contents.text: The details in the passage support this inference about Thoreau's experience at Walden Pond:

text.text: His life of simplicity and self-reliance challenges the societal norms of materialism and constant work.

content.text: Thoreau describes how he lives alone, builds his own home, and relies on his labor, highlighting a life of simplicity contrary to the societal expectations of acquiring more property and possessions through constant work.

contents.text: The details in the passage do not support these inferences:

text.text: His life of isolation and loneliness contrasts with the societal standard of supporting many children.

content.text: While the passage details Thoreau's solitary lifestyle, it does not discuss societal standards regarding family size or imply that his lifestyle is a direct contrast to having many children.

text.text: His life in a house that he builds himself differs from the societal aspiration to inherit existing family homes.

content.text: While Thoreau mentions building his own home, the passage does not compare this to societal aspirations about inheriting homes.

text.text: His life far away from his family calls into question his neighbors' societal choice to remain in Concord for generations.

content.text: The passage does not mention Thoreau's distance from family or critique his neighbors' choices to stay in Concord, focusing instead on his personal decisions and philosophical reflections.

contents.text: If one of these elements does not apply to the type of work being cited, or if the information is missing, that element is left out.
Here are examples of how MLA citations can look:
Here is more information about each of the elements:

meaning.text: This is the name (or names) of the work's creator(s). The first author's name is written in last name, first name format (Smith, Jane). If there is a second author, his or her name is written in first name last name format (Smith, Jane, and John Doe). If there are three or more authors, the first author's name is followed by "et al.," which stands for "and others" (Smith, Jane, et al.).

This is the title of what you are citing, such as the title of a book. If the source is an entire work, the title appears in italics. If the source is part of a larger work or collection, the title appears in quotation marks. This might be the title of an article, essay, poem, short story, or web page.

When applicable, this is the title of the larger work or collection that the source is a part of. It appears in italics. This might be the title of a book or the name of a newspaper, journal, magazine, or website.
These are other people who helped create the work, such as editors or translators. The citation explains the contributor's role (edited by John Doe).
This is usually the work's edition number (9th ed.).
This is usually the volume number, issue number, or both (vol. 10, no. 15).
This is the company that published the work. If the work is a website that has the same name as the publisher, the publisher element is usually left out.
This is the date when the work was published.
This is the page number(s) (p. 3, pp. 3–5) or web page address where the source was found.

This is the date when a web page was viewed. The date of access is optional, but authors often include it if the publication date for a web page is unknown. Authors might also include a date of access if a web page has changed or no longer exists.

If there are three or more authors, the first author's name is followed by "et al.," which stands for "and others" (Smith, Jane, et al.).

This is the title of what you are citing, such as the title of a book. If the source is an entire work, the title appears in italics. If the source is part of a larger work or collection, the title appears in quotation marks. This might be the title of an article, essay, poem, short story, or web page.

When applicable, this is the title of the larger work or collection that the source is a part of. It appears in italics. This might be the title of a book or the name of a newspaper, journal, magazine, or website.
These are other people who helped create the work, such as editors or translators. The citation explains the contributor's role (edited by John Doe).
This is usually the work's edition number (9th ed.).
This is usually the volume number, issue number, or both (vol. 10, no. 15).
This is the company that published the work. If the work is a website that has the same name as the publisher, the publisher element is usually left out.
This is the date when the work was published.
This is the page number(s) (p. 3, pp. 3–5) or web page address where the source was found.

This is the date when a web page was viewed. The date of access is optional, but authors often include it if the publication date for a web page is unknown. Authors might also include a date of access if a web page has changed or no longer exists.

lessons.name: Identify and correct inappropriate shifts in verb tense

header.text: Does the following text have an inappropriate shift in verb tense? If so, fix any verbs that don't match the tense of the verb in bold. If not, submit the text without making any changes.
The tense of a verb tells when the action takes place. You should generally avoid shifting tenses within or between sentences unless you need to reflect a time change.

text.text: Kathy grew up in Cleveland, but now she lives in Pittsburgh.

explanationText.text: The sentence shifts to present tense to reflect a time change.

text.text: Rachel grabbed the microphone and speaks to the crowd.

pieces.text: There is no need to reflect a time change, so both verbs should be in the same tense.

header.text: However, you may shift tenses if you need to use the present tense to state a general truth. You may also shift to the present tense to discuss the nature or contents of an artistic work, such as a book, film, or painting. This use of the present tense is called the literary present tense.

text.text: Mr. Smith taught his students that the brain uses around 20% of the body's energy.

explanationText.text: The sentence shifts to present tense to state a general truth.

text.text: Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet in the late 1500s, but the play explores themes that are still relevant today.

explanationText.text: The sentence shifts to the literary present tense to discuss the nature of an artistic work.
